data.title: Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs (TRIAD): study design and rationale for a prospective, parallel-group, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial of rapamycin in healthy middle-aged dogs from the Dog Aging Project
data.authors: Coleman AE; Creevy KE; Kaeberlein M

evidence.label: Registered trial, no results yet
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Companion dogs, RCT (ongoing, Dog Aging Project, middle-aged healthy dogs)
data.finding: Design and rationale paper (protocol), NOT results. TRIAD is a double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial testing whether rapamycin prolongs lifespan and improves healthspan measures in healthy middle-aged dogs from the Dog Aging Project. Its authors describe it as the first rigorous test of a drug against biological aging with lifespan and healthspan endpoints performed outside the laboratory in any species. Planned size is 580 dogs with 3 years of treatment (NIH-funded, per Texas A&M announcement; 170 dogs enrolled at that time). No efficacy or safety results exist yet, so this must not be cited as evidence of benefit.
data.abstract_excerpt: Companion dogs are a powerful model for aging research given their morphologic and genetic variability, risk for age-related disease, and habitation of the human environment. In addition, the shorter life expectancy of dogs compared to human beings provides a unique opportunity for an accelerated timeline to test interventions that might extend healthy lifespan.

extracted_findings.species: Companion dogs - RCT (design paper, ongoing, no results yet)
extracted_findings.effect: No results yet - first placebo-controlled lifespan trial of rapamycin outside the lab (dogs)
